setting: an HR analytics platform sold to mid-size manufacturers (Peoplegrid)
prompt: I’m the senior product manager for Peoplegrid, the HR analytics platform we sell to mid‑size manufacturers. On March 1 2024 we launched a new onboarding workflow aimed at reducing churn. In the first two months we saw 2,450 active users, an activation rate of 68% (we need 75% to hit our forecast), and churn of 9% for Q2 (target 5% for Q3). To test a new “quick‑start” tutorial we ran an A/B experiment from June 5‑19 2024 with 1,200 users in control (12% conversion to “fully configured”) and 1,250 in variant (14% conversion). We’re assuming the only driver of churn is onboarding completion, and we’ve calculated the lift as a 30% relative increase, although the arithmetic actually reflects a 2‑point absolute gain on a 12% base. We still don’t know the average support cost per employee after rollout, which could affect ROI. I need a concise answer for our COO, Maya Patel: (1) what single North‑Star metric we should adopt next to steer the product, (2) the three biggest ways this data‑driven plan could fail, and (3) what specific result (e.g., a drop below X% conversion or a cost per support ticket above Y) would make us stop or pivot the initiative.

setting: a podcast hosting and ad-marketplace company (Echolane)
prompt: I’m sending this to you as the product lead for Echolane, and the answer needs to be a concise recommendation for our CEO, Maya Patel. Yesterday we finished a two‑week A/B test (14 days, from May 3 to May 16) of a new mid‑roll ad slot. Variant B received 120,000 impressions and generated 3,840 clicks (3.2 % CTR) and $45,200 in revenue; the control got 115,000 impressions, 3,220 clicks (2.8 % CTR) and $38,500 revenue. We assumed the new pricing tier would stay flat for the next quarter and that the higher CTR would translate directly into higher CPM without affecting listener churn. What we don’t know yet is the impact on subscriber churn over the next three months, nor the incremental server cost of serving the extra ads (we only have a rough $7 k estimate). Please give me one clear recommendation on whether to roll out the slot globally, outline the main ways this rollout could fail (e.g., churn, cost overruns, brand safety), and specify what result—such as a churn increase above 1.5 % or a cost per impression rise above $0.08—would make us stop or pivot.

setting: a veterinary clinic chain (Pawprint Vets)
prompt: I’m the regional ops lead for Pawprint Vets and need a clear go‑no‑go recommendation for Dr. Maya Patel, our founder‑CEO. From July 1‑31 2024 we ran an A/B test on a new automated SMS reminder system for follow‑up appointments. The control group had 2,800 scheduled visits and a 38% show‑up rate (1,064 attended); the variant had 2,200 scheduled visits and a 44% show‑up rate (968 attended). We’re assuming the uplift in attendance will translate directly into a 15% increase in average procedure revenue per visit, which we estimate at $120. The SMS vendor charges $0.04 per message, and we sent an average of 1.3 messages per appointment. The test cost us $2,600 in messages, but we haven’t yet accounted for the integration development time, which we estimate at 80 hours at $150/hour. The unknown is the longer‑term churn: we don’t know how many of these extra visits will become repeat customers after the first 30 days. I need one recommendation on whether to roll the reminder system chain‑wide, the main ways this rollout could fail (e.g., integration bugs, patient pushback, hidden costs), and the specific result that would make us stop or pivot (e.g., net profit negative after three months). Please also flag any arithmetic or assumption errors you spot.

setting: an online used-furniture marketplace (Second Seat)
prompt: I’m writing to you on behalf of our CEO, Maya Patel, because we need a clear go‑no‑go recommendation on the pricing experiment we ran for our “Second Seat Premium” listing tier. From March 1 to March 28 we showed 12,542 unique visitors a new $19.99 “Fast‑Track” shipping option; 1,874 of them clicked the upgrade, and 842 completed a purchase at the $299 average basket size, versus a baseline conversion of 3.4 % and $267 basket size on the standard tier. We assumed the extra $32 per order would offset the $5 shipping subsidy we’re offering, and we also assumed the uplift would sustain for at least 90 days. The unknown is whether this higher‑price tier will cannibalize repeat purchases in the next quarter; we have no data on churn impact yet. Please give Maya one recommendation on whether to roll this tier out nationwide, list the main ways this decision could fail (e.g., cost overruns, brand perception, churn), and identify the specific result (e.g., weekly net revenue dip > 5 % for two consecutive weeks) that would make us stop or change course.

setting: a construction-bid estimating tool (Cornerstone Bids)
prompt: I’m the senior product manager for Cornerstone Bids and need a clear call for our Chief Product Officer, Maya Patel. Yesterday we wrapped a four‑week A/B test (April 1–28) of the new “Project Forecast” pricing tier against the current “Standard” tier. We exposed 2,500 active users (1,250 per variant). The test showed 92 sign‑ups on Forecast versus 78 on Standard, which we calculated as a 17.9 % lift (I’ve added the percentages). Revenue per new sign‑up was $1,200 for Forecast and $1,050 for Standard, giving $110,400 versus $81,900 in expected revenue. We assumed the higher sign‑up rate will translate directly into a proportional increase in quarterly revenue, and we’ve not yet factored any additional support cost; we estimate an extra $0.10 per user per month for the new tier, but that’s a rough guess. The unknown is the churn rate after 90 days for Forecast users – we have no data yet. Also, the test period coincided with a regional construction boom that boosted overall activity by roughly 8 % compared with the same period last year, which we haven’t adjusted for. Please give Maya one recommendation on whether to roll out Forecast nationwide, outline the principal ways this decision could fail (including any hidden risks), and specify what result—e.g., churn above X % or support cost over Y %—would make us stop or pivot.

setting: a wine-subscription direct-to-consumer brand (Vinelet)
prompt: I’m the head of growth at Vinelet, our direct‑to‑consumer wine‑subscription brand, and I need a concise brief for our CMO, Maya Patel. From March 5 to March 20 we ran an A/B test on the post‑checkout upsell page. The control group had 12,000 visitors and a purchase conversion of 4.2 % (504 orders). The variant showed the new “Reserve Club” badge and attracted 11,500 visitors with a conversion of 4.8 % (552 orders). Each order generates $84 of revenue, and the new badge adds a packaging surcharge of $2 per unit. I’m assuming that the $2 cost is fully absorbed by the existing margin and does not affect churn. What I don’t know yet is the 60‑day churn impact of the badge. The raw numbers suggest an incremental revenue of $2,592, but I suspect a calculation error there. Please give me one recommendation on whether to roll out the badge, list the primary ways this rollout could fail, and tell me what specific outcome (e.g., churn rise above 1.5 % or net revenue lift under $1,500) would make us stop or pivot.

setting: a city transit agency's rider-information app team (Metro Line Digital)

setting: a developer-tools company selling a CI accelerator (Quickbuild)
prompt: I’m pulling together the latest A/B test results for Quickbuild’s new “Instant Cache” feature and need a clear call for Maya Patel, our VP of Product. setting: a K-12 school-district software vendor (Maple Learning Systems)
prompt:
Tara,

setting: an insurance broker adding a self-serve quote tool (Anchor Mutual Brokers)
prompt: I’m the product lead on the new self‑serve quote tool at Anchor Mutual Brokers and need a clear next step to brief Raj Patel, our CEO, on the A/B test we just finished. setting: a boutique fitness studio chain (Tempo Studios)
prompt: I’m sending this to the AI on behalf of Maya Patel, our CFO, because we need a clear go‑no‑go recommendation for the new class‑schedule rollout. Over the two‑week test (June 1 – June 14) we emailed 5,000 of our active members: 2,800 received version A (the current schedule) and 2,200 received version B (the proposed staggered schedule). setting: a nonprofit food bank scaling a donor program (Greater Valley Food Bank)
prompt: I ran an email drive on September 1 2024 to 10,000 households, spending $10,000 on list procurement and design. I’m assuming the cost per acquisition is $12.5 for email ($10,000/800) and $8 for text ($2,000/250), and I’m also assuming donors from text are more likely to become recurring because a small pilot last quarter showed a 12% recurring rate versus 5% for email. setting: a regional grocery delivery startup (Tidewater Fresh)
prompt: Hi AI, I need a quick read on the A/B test we ran on the new delivery fee structure so I can brief our CEO Maya Patel tomorrow. Thanks.

setting: a payroll software company for small restaurants (Acme Payroll)
prompt: I need a quick read‑out for Carla Jensen, our board member, on the A/B test we ran on the new onboarding flow for restaurant owners. setting: a pediatric telehealth clinic network (Northwind Kids Health)
prompt: I’m the product lead for Northwind Kids Health and need a clear call for Dr. Maya Patel, our Chief Medical Officer, on whether to roll out the new video‑triage widget after the pilot A/B test we ran from Jan 5 to Jan 25. setting: a 40-person logistics software company selling to freight brokers (Brightline Freight)
prompt: I’m sending this to you on behalf of Ravi, our founder, who needs a clear go‑no‑go on the A/B test we ran on the new “Freight‑Flex” pricing tier. Over the past 14 days we showed the tier to 3,600 active broker accounts (1,800 in control, 1,800 in treatment). setting: a consumer budgeting app with a free tier (Pennywise)
prompt:

setting: an industrial sensor maker moving into subscriptions (Ferrous Sensing)
prompt: I need a clear call for Elena Torres, our CEO, on whether we should roll out the $150‑per‑month subscription tier we tested last quarter or stick with the $120 tier. setting: a meal-kit company for athletes (Ironplate Meals)
prompt: I’m pulling together the final deck for Maya Patel, our CEO, and I need a clear call on the “Protein Plus” add‑on we tested last month. From 2024‑09‑01 to 2024‑09‑30 we ran an A/B test on 12,000 eligible Ironplate Meals orders (6,000 control, 6,000 variant). The variant showed a 4.8% lift in average order value (from $84.12 to $88.03) and a 2.1% increase in repeat purchase within 14 days (from 18.0% to 20.1%). Revenue from the variant cohort was $528,180 versus $504,720 in control, a $23,460 difference. We assumed the additional $3.91 per order would not affect churn, and we’re budgeting an extra $0.45 per unit for packaging, but the exact incremental shipping cost is still unknown. The marketing spend for the test was $12,000, and the projected rollout cost is $45,000 per month for creatives and $0.30 per unit for fulfillment. Please give me one recommendation on whether to launch nationally, outline the three biggest ways this rollout could fail, and specify the result or metric that would make us halt or pivot the program. Keep the answer framed for Maya.

setting: a legal-document automation startup for solo lawyers (Clause & Co)
prompt: Hey AI, I’m Dan, the product lead at Clause & Co, and I need a concise decision brief for our founder and CEO Maya Patel. Over the past 28 days we ran an A/B test on the new “Smart Clause Builder” onboarding flow (Variant A) versus the existing flow (Variant B). Variant A had 3,200 unique solo‑lawyer sign‑ups, 800 of whom completed their first document; Variant B had 2,900 sign‑ups with 640 completions. We’re seeing a conversion of 25 % for A vs 22 % for B, which we calculated as a 3‑point lift (actually 3.0 % absolute but we wrote 3 % relative). The average revenue per completed document is $45, and the acquisition cost for both groups is $30 per sign‑up. The test cost us $87,000 in paid ads. Assume the monthly subscription price stays at $49 and that the churn rate will stay constant at 5 % month‑over‑month. The unknown is how these early completions will translate into 90‑day LTV and whether any support overhead will rise with the new flow. Please give Maya one recommendation on whether to roll out Variant A, list the main ways the rollout could fail (e.g., hidden support costs, churn increase, traffic quality shift), and specify what result (e.g., < 1 % lift in 30‑day revenue or a rise in support tickets > 15 %) would make us stop or change course.

setting: a hospital outpatient scheduling team (St. Mara Outpatient)
prompt: I’m the scheduling lead for St. Mara Outpatient and need a crisp briefing for Dr. Lena Ortiz, our Chief Medical Officer, by Friday. We ran an A/B test on two reminder workflows for upcoming appointments. Variant A (standard SMS) was sent to 4,200 patients between 3 Mar and 10 Mar, yielding 1,158 confirmed appointments (27.6% completion). Variant B (personalized voice call) reached 4,250 patients from 11 Mar to 18 Mar and recorded 1,210 confirmed appointments (28.5% completion). We assumed that higher confirmation directly reduces no‑shows and improves patient satisfaction, which we’ll measure later. The cost per SMS is $0.05, per voice call $0.22; we haven’t captured the total labor expense for the calls yet (unknown). Also note the 72‑hour window between reminder and appointment is the same for both variants, but we didn’t track whether patients who confirmed still cancelled later. Please give me one clear recommendation on which workflow to roll out system‑wide, list the main ways this decision could fail (e.g., hidden costs, patient preference shifts), and specify the result—such as a sustained no‑show rate above 12%—that would make us stop or pivot the approach.

setting: a fleet-electrification consultancy (Voltway Advisors)
prompt: I’m sending this to you on behalf of our CEO, Alana Patel, at Voltway Advisors. We just wrapped a three‑month pilot (Jan 15 – Apr 14 2024) to electrify 120 of our client’s delivery vans. The upfront cost per electric van was $45,000 versus $30,000 for a comparable diesel unit. We’ve logged a maintenance saving of $3,500 per vehicle each month and a fuel‑cost reduction of $2,000 per month, which we’ve summed to $9,500 in monthly savings per van (assumption: electricity price stays flat). During the pilot, 85 % of the vans achieved the 90 % uptime target; however, four vans experienced more than 12 hours of downtime due to charging bottlenecks. Driver‑satisfaction scores rose to 78 compared with a baseline of 65. The unknown is the longer‑term battery degradation cost after 12 months, plus any impact on revenue from the downtime incidents. Please give me one clear recommendation for Alana on whether to roll out the program fleet‑wide, outline the main ways this rollout could fail, and tell me what result (e.g., a specific drop in uptime or cost overrun) would make us stop or change course.
